label: Drinks
rationale: Water, coffee, alcohol and tea all take nomu. These are the four drinks people offer and ask about every day.
mixUps: All four take nomu, so drill them in one frame (mizu nomu? koohii nomu?); medicine and soup take nomu too. Making the tea or coffee is ocha o ireru (in Breakfast), never ocha o tsukuru.

targets.use: Often heard as care and advice, after drinking alcohol or in the heat: mizu nonda? (have you had some water?), mizu nonde ne (make sure you drink water). Also when thirsty: nodo kawaita, mizu nomitai (I'm thirsty, I want some water). Casual speech drops o.
targets.notes: mizu is cold or room-temperature water; hot water is oyu, not atsui mizu. In restaurants ask for omizu, which is free. In polite heat warnings you hear komame ni suibun o totte kudasai (keep taking fluids).

example.romaji: atsui kara, mizu chanto nonde ne.
example.ja: 暑いから、水ちゃんと飲んでね。
example.english: It's hot, so make sure you drink enough water.

examplePolite.romaji: atsui node, omizu o chanto nonde kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 暑いので、お水をちゃんと飲んでくださいね。
examplePolite.english: It's hot, so please make sure you drink enough water.

targets.use: Used to offer a cup and to talk about habits: koohii nomu? (want a coffee?), koohii wa nomanai (I don't drink coffee). Casual speech drops o, and koohii demo nomu? (a coffee or something?) softens an invitation.
targets.notes: To order, say koohii (o) onegaishimasu or koohii ni shimasu (I'll have coffee). Making it is koohii o ireru.

example.romaji: asa wa koohii nomanai to dame na n da.
example.ja: 朝はコーヒー飲まないとダメなんだ。
example.english: I can't get going in the morning without coffee.

examplePolite.romaji: asa wa koohii o nomanai to dame na n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 朝はコーヒーを飲まないとダメなんです。
examplePolite.english: I can't get going in the morning without coffee.

targets.trap: Learners take osake to mean Japanese sake, but it covers any alcohol, beer and wine included; rice wine is nihonshu.
targets.use: Used to ask about and describe drinking: osake nomu? or osake nomeru? (do you drink?), anmari nomanai (I don't drink much). Casual speech drops o, and once drinking is the topic nomu alone means alcohol: kinou nomisugita (I drank too much last night).
targets.notes: nomi ni iku (go out for drinks) and nomikai (a drinking party) use the same nomu. How much you can take is osake ni tsuyoi / osake ni yowai, casually osake yowai n da (I'm a lightweight). Bare sake (sake nomou ze) is rougher, mostly male speech; osake is the everyday default for everyone.

example.romaji: kyou kuruma da kara, osake wa nomenai.
example.ja: 今日車だから、お酒は飲めない。
example.english: I'm driving today, so I can't drink.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kuruma na node, osake wa nomenai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は車なので、お酒は飲めないんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm driving today, so I can't drink.

targets.trap: English 'tea' means black tea, but ocha is green or other Japanese tea (mugicha, houjicha); black tea, with or without milk, is koucha.
targets.use: Said at home and at work, and as a soft offer or invitation: ocha demo nomu? (fancy a cup of tea?). Casual speech drops o, and ocha means whatever Japanese tea is on hand, including cold mugicha.
targets.notes: ocha ni shiyou / ocha ni shimashou ka (let's stop for tea) is the usual way to call a tea break. ocha shinai? / ocha shiyou (go for tea) means a café break, coffee included. Making the tea is ocha o ireru.

example.romaji: chotto kyuukei shite, ocha demo nomou.
example.ja: ちょっと休憩して、お茶でも飲もう。
example.english: Let's take a short break and have some tea.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto kyuukei shite, ocha demo nomimashou.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと休憩して、お茶でも飲みましょう。
examplePolite.english: Let's take a short break and have some tea.
